e1.reason: The statement concerns reading 1/b from a partition that is given; the assessment hands over an already partitioned rectangle. Being able to construct an equal-area partition for any b is not needed to understand what 1/b names.

e3.reason: The half/third/fourth names are the special cases b = 2, 3, 4 of the unit-fraction name 1/b. A learner can meet 1/b directly from equal partitions without the vocabulary words.

e4.reason: The statement already says the whole is partitioned into b equal parts, so exhaustion of the whole is built into the partition idea (and into partitioning.equal-shares.area). Knowing that b copies make the whole is used later (b/b = 1), not to name one part as 1/b.

e7.reason: The target is the measure facet. A measure-first route reaches 1/b on the line from unit length: partition 0-1 into b equal lengths and see that b copies of the piece fill the unit, with no area-model unit fraction.
e7.other_route: Measure-first (Davydov/Measure Up style): from number-line.whole-number-lengths and equal-length partitioning, name the piece 1/b because b copies of it make the unit length.

e9.reason: Direction is reversed: partitioning.equal-area.any-shape uses 'partition one side into n equal lengths' as its own step 1, which is exactly the skill the target's step 2 needs. The shared prerequisite is an equal-length partition of a segment, not the area procedure.

e10.reason: The target is the measure facet and its statement is a copies of the length 1/b from 0. This is reachable from fraction.unit.number-line by iterating the unit-fraction length, without the area-model reading of a/b.
e10.other_route: From fraction.unit.number-line, iterate the located length 1/b a times from 0 (measure-first route).

e20.reason: The shaded regions in the standard bar/strip models of 1/2 and 2/4 are congruent, so the 'same amount, different shape' idea is not needed to judge them equal. It helps when models differ in shape. The rationale also misreads the source, which is about equal shares of identical wholes having different shapes, not about parts of different sizes.

e28.reason: The explanation can be given without splitting: draw two equal-size bars, shade 1/2 on one and 2/4 on the other, and show they cover the same amount using the same-size criterion.
e28.other_route: Draw two aligned equal bars showing 1/2 and 2/4 and compare the shaded amounts directly (fraction.equivalent.same-size plus fraction.non-unit.part-whole).

e33.reason: The target is measure facet. The idea that a fractions are a copies of one common size 1/b is already given by fraction.non-unit.number-line (a lengths of 1/b from 0); the part-whole reading is the same idea in an area model.
e33.other_route: Compare on the number line via fraction.non-unit.number-line: more lengths of the same size 1/b lie farther from 0.

e40.reason: Understanding that an amount depends on which whole needs only the meaning of a unit fraction (e41) and direct size comparison (e39). The rule 1/2 > 1/3 is the misconception being qualified, not a requirement for seeing that wholes can differ in size.

e50.reason: The same-whole requirement enters through the justification-by-drawing node; the story simply states the pizzas are the same size, so solving it does not require the caveat as a separate concept.

e52.reason: The symbolic pattern can be noticed from several number-line examples (2/3 and 4/6, 1/2 and 3/6, ...) where a finer partition keeps the same point, which fraction.equivalent.same-point already supplies.
e52.other_route: Generalize from number-line partitions: refine each 1/b length into n equal lengths and see the same point (via fraction.equivalent.same-point).

e53.reason: At level 3 the learner needs to understand what n x a means, but the equal-groups reading is not the only way: the product as an array (rows by columns) gives the same understanding.
e53.other_route: Multiplication understood as an array or rectangular area (rows x columns), then the rule applied to the products.

e54.reason: Only the test items (3 x 4, 5 x 4, etc.) need recalled products; the principle itself holds for any whole number n.

e63.reason: The simple explain node is the special case n = 2 (and similar) of the general argument. The target's own assessment already requires a specific model case (2/3 = 8/12) plus the generalization, so the special case is not a separate prerequisite.

e65.reason: The count of pieces can be described as 'n times as many' (parts and chosen parts each become n times as many), which gives n x a and n x b without invoking commutativity.
e65.other_route: Describe the refinement as n times as many parts and n times as many chosen parts (multiplicative comparison, multiplication.comparison).

e73.reason: The idea (n equal shares make exactly the whole) does not depend on the words halves, thirds, fourths; only the examples and the test question phrase it that way.

e76.reason: The idea that more equal shares of the same whole are smaller does not need the names; the assessment happens to ask about a half and a fourth.

e77.reason: At level 1 the claim can be established by directly comparing a half and a fourth cut from same-size wholes. The explanation via 'the shares always make the same whole' is a justification, not required to hold the concept.
e77.other_route: Cut same-size wholes into 2, 3, 4 shares and compare the shares by direct comparison (comparing.size.direct).

e80.reason: The concept is about equal shares of identical wholes having different shapes; the word 'half' appears only in the test question.

e81.reason: The idea needs only perceiving that the shapes differ; naming or classifying triangles and rectangles is used by the test wording.

e83.reason: Equal-length partition of a side by laying unit lengths only works when the side length is a multiple of n units. Other credible ways: folding or marking the side and checking by direct comparison, or measuring the side and dividing.
e83.other_route: Partition the side by folding or by trial marking checked with direct comparison of the pieces (comparing.size.direct).

e92.reason: The statement needs only the idea of length as a number of unit lengths (e93). The test can be done on a given line with equally spaced labeled points, so iterating units is helpful for building the number line but not required.

e97.reason: The procedure allows one jump or any smaller jumps. Jumping by ones, or any chunk, represents the sum; tens-and-ones splitting only makes the computation efficient.

e99.reason: The jump of b can be taken in one move or in any smaller moves; place-value chunks (10 and 7) are an efficiency, not required to represent the difference.

e105.reason: The step allows one jump or smaller jumps; going to the next ten then by tens is a strategy choice, not required for the representation.

e112.reason: The partitive meaning can be learned from dealing out objects one at a time into b groups (sharing), which uses counting and the idea of equal groups and no multiplication.
e112.other_route: Equal sharing by dealing out objects one by one (CGI sharing problems), then counting what is in each group.

e114.reason: The measurement meaning can be learned by repeatedly taking groups of b from a and counting the groups (repeated subtraction), without a multiplication meaning.
e114.other_route: Repeatedly remove groups of b from the a objects and count how many groups are formed.

e119.reason: Alternative sources for the multiplication/division link exist: the partitive meaning or an array. At least one division meaning is needed, so an OR-clause {division.measurement.meaning, division.partitive.meaning} fits.
e119.other_route: Partitive meaning (division.partitive.meaning): b groups of c make a, or a rows-by-columns array with one dimension unknown.

e120.reason: Same as the measurement-meaning edge: either division meaning (or an array) can ground the unknown-factor reading. At least one of the two is needed; an OR-clause fits.
e120.other_route: Measurement meaning (division.measurement.meaning): c groups of b make a, or a rows-by-columns array with one dimension unknown.

e121.reason: The multiplication equation b x c = a only needs a multiplication meaning; the array/area meaning serves equally.
e121.other_route: Read b x c = a as an array with b rows and c columns containing a objects.

e122.reason: Commutativity is needed only on the grouping route (c groups of b gives c x b). The partitive route gives b groups of c, which is b x c directly, and the fact can be stated in either factor order.
e122.other_route: Use the partitive reading (b groups of c make a) so the equation is b x c = a without reordering.

e124.reason: The unknown-factor meaning enters through the rewrite step (a divided by b = ? becomes b x ? = a), which is the only place the procedure uses it. The existence remark (b not 0, a a multiple of b) is commentary, not performed.

missing_prerequisites.why: The denominator b is found by counting the equal parts (the test item has 6 parts); no route reads b without counting or an equivalent.

Step 2 partitions the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal lengths. No node in the map teaches equal-length partitioning of a segment (folding, marking, checking by comparison); the area procedure uses it rather than supplies it.

missing_routes.description: Measure-first route: name 1/b as the length whose b copies make the unit length, built from lengths on the number line rather than from the area-model unit fraction.
Measure-first route: iterate the located unit-fraction length a times from 0 with no area-model non-unit fraction.
Explain by drawing two aligned equal-size bars with 1/2 and 2/4 shaded and comparing the shaded amounts directly, without the splitting procedure.
Understand n x a and n x b through the array (rows by columns) meaning of multiplication instead of equal groups.

missing_prerequisites.why: The visual model of 2/3 and then 8/12 must show a shaded parts out of b equal parts; the assessment requires drawing it.
The argument is a splitting of every part into n equal smaller parts, an equal partition of a part of a shape.
Step 1 partitions a side into n equal lengths for any n; the map has no node that teaches this.

missing_routes.description: Dealing-out route: share objects one at a time among b groups and count what each group gets, with no multiplication.
Repeated-removal route: take groups of b from a until none remain and count the groups, with no multiplication.
Array route: read b x c = a as an array with b rows and c columns and a total of a, with one dimension unknown.
